title: Map the cosmic dark ages and first luminous structures in three dimensions

concept.text: The innovation is validated three-dimensional mapping of the early Universe through the redshifted 21-cm signal from neutral hydrogen. Observations would recover spatial variations in 21-cm brightness temperature across the sky and across redshift, revealing how structure changed over cosmic time. The goal is to resolve an evolving cosmic volume, extending beyond a sky-averaged measurement or a statistical estimate of fluctuations.

Brightness temperature is the observable; a map does not directly identify every gas property or luminous object. Its interpretation depends on physical modelling of gas conditions and radiation backgrounds. During cosmic dawn and reionisation, those conditions carry the collective imprint of the first luminous sources. The concept also encompasses the earlier dark ages, but the supplied evidence directly grounds the mapping case for cosmic dawn and reionisation and does not establish comparable observational reach into the earlier era.

significance.text: Successful spatial recovery across redshift would make a poorly observed period accessible as an evolving three-dimensional volume. Researchers could examine where early structure developed and how radiation from emerging sources affected surrounding hydrogen. The revolutionary advance would be access to the spatial organisation and evolution of that field, beyond detecting its average behaviour or measuring the aggregate strength of fluctuations.

Interpreted through physical models, such maps could constrain early gas conditions and the populations responsible for the radiation signatures. Their scientific value would depend on which spatial scales and redshifts were recovered reliably. Observing a brightness-temperature pattern would not by itself uniquely determine the properties of its sources, and extending the impact claim from cosmic dawn to the earlier dark ages requires additional evidence about achievable coverage.

Conceptual synthesis: this would provide environmental context for discoveries of the first stars and early massive black holes. Combining a mapped hydrogen environment with independently identified objects could help test explanations of their influence. Those downstream possibilities depend on suitable overlapping observations and successful interpretation; a hydrogen map alone would not establish the identity of individual first-generation stars or resolve how the earliest black holes formed.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable recovery of the cosmological 21-cm brightness-temperature field as spatially resolved maps over multiple redshift intervals. A statistical upper limit constrains how large fluctuations could be without recovering their locations. A sky-averaged measurement follows the mean signal with redshift without locating structure across the sky. Tomography requires enough sensitivity and control of contamination to retain spatial information as well as spectral information.

The cosmological signal is faint relative to foreground radio emission. Radio-frequency interference, ionospheric scintillation and instrumental calibration errors further complicate its recovery. The engineering challenge includes collecting sufficiently sensitive observations and calibrating the instrument accurately enough that contamination does not masquerade as cosmological structure. The analysis must also distinguish foreground removal from inadvertent removal or distortion of the desired signal.

A further unresolved step is demonstrating that validation methods support map recovery. The reviewed NenuFAR study injected simulated signals before foreground removal to assess bias in recovered power spectra within specified signal families. That is useful evidence about the analysis pipeline, but it does not establish faithful recovery of a three-dimensional cosmological image. Map-level fidelity, robustness to different plausible signals and coverage of the earlier dark ages remain additional requirements.

current_state.text: Munshi and colleagues reported in 2025 that four nights of NenuFAR observations yielded upper limits on cosmic-dawn 21-cm fluctuations in bins centred at redshifts 17.0 and 20.3. The abstract describes power-spectrum upper limits, and the supplied full-text review records an explicit non-detection of the cosmological signal. This result therefore demonstrates an upper-limit measurement at those redshifts, not a recovered three-dimensional cosmological map.

The arXiv landing page lists a 2025 journal reference associated with DOI 10.1093/mnras/staf1386. The supplied review distinguishes that bibliographic information from preprint and placeholder acceptance information in the PDF. It also distinguishes foreground images and intermediate data cubes from cosmological tomography: producing those analysis products does not establish detection or mapping of the underlying cosmological field.

The reviewed paper describes tomographic mapping as a prospective capability associated with increased sensitivity, including discussion of the upcoming SKA. Such prospects are projections rather than demonstrated maps. The supplied review draws on both an abstract-bearing landing page and a complete 23-page text extraction, so the assessment is not restricted to abstract access. However, the supplied freshness record is empty: it does not establish the latest field-wide state through 2026-11-01 or assess subsequent achievements. That gap limits claims about present-day progress; it is not evidence that later results do not exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently calibrated observations should recover consistent spatial maps of cosmological 21-cm brightness temperature across multiple redshift intervals. The recovered field should resolve evolving structure over a volume large enough to support the stated scientific conclusions. Before assessing success, investigators would need to specify the required volume, spatial resolution, redshift coverage, uncertainty and observing effort. These are proposed criteria; the supplied evidence does not establish numerical thresholds or a consensus completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: realistic signal-injection tests should quantify how calibration and foreground treatment alter recovered structure, including signal loss, bias and false features. The NenuFAR paper provides a methodological basis through injections used to assess power-spectrum recovery, but convincing tomography would require extending validation to the maps themselves. Testing should cover several plausible signal structures rather than demonstrating recovery only for a narrow simulated family.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed validation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent reductions and, where feasible, independent observations should reproduce the main structures within stated uncertainties. Comparisons with independent tracers should be used where suitable observations exist. Results should disclose the scales and redshifts that remain inaccessible, the sensitivity of conclusions to physical modelling and the observing resources required. A demonstration confined to cosmic dawn or reionisation should be described at that scope; earlier dark-ages coverage requires its own evidence. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth and reliability within those boundaries, not universal recovery under every possible condition.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AST-11, “Identify the first generation of metal-free stars,” has the closest direct overlap. AST-06 concerns the spatial hydrogen field and the collective effects of early radiation sources; AST-11 concerns identifying a particular stellar population. A mapped radiation imprint would not alone identify individual metal-free stars, while identifying those stars would not itself produce volumetric hydrogen maps. Only the AST-11 title is supplied, so its detailed requirements and precise overlap remain unassessed.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-13, “Establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew,” shares the early-source setting. Hydrogen tomography could potentially provide environmental and radiation context relevant to explanations of early black-hole growth. Establishing their formation and growth history would require additional evidence connecting those environments to the black holes themselves; neither concept completes the other.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-05, “Detect and identify a primordial gravitational-wave background,” and AST-12, “Directly detect the cosmic neutrino background,” also seek observational access to cosmic history through different signals. Their overlap with AST-06 is the broader ambition of opening difficult observational windows. Their observables and completion requirements remain distinct from mapping the high-redshift hydrogen brightness-temperature field.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-08, “Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets,” shares the requirement to demonstrate reliable spatial reconstruction. Its target is a planetary surface, whereas AST-06 seeks an evolving cosmological volume. AST-03 and AST-04, concerning the constituent of dark matter and the cause of cosmic acceleration, could potentially benefit from additional cosmological observations, but successful 21-cm tomography would not by itself establish either physical explanation.
